title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 102
paragraphs: For the Athenians and those ranged next to them, numbering perhaps half the whole army, the route lay along the sea-beach and over level ground, while the Lacedaemonians and those ranged with them were compelled to go through a ravine and along the mountainside. So while the Lacedaemonians were still going around, those on the other wing were already beginning the fight. As long as the Persians' wicker shields still remained upright, they continued to defend themselves and rather had the advantage in the fight; but when the Athenians and those ranged next to them, wanting the achievement to belong to them and not to the Lacedaemonians, with exhortations to one another set themselves more vigorously to the work, then from that point the fortune of the fight changed. They pushed aside the wicker shields and fell upon the Persians in a single rush; the Persians sustained their first attack and continued to defend themselves for a long time, but at last fled to the wall. The Athenians, Corinthians, Sikyonians, and Troizenians — for that was the order of their ranks — followed close after them and rushed in together with them into the space within the wall. When the wall too was captured, the barbarians no longer turned to resistance but began to take flight — all except the Persians, who formed into small groups and continued to fight the Greeks as they rushed in within the wall. Of the Persian commanders, two escaped and two were slain: Artaÿntes and Ithamitres, commanders of the fleet, escaped, while Mardontes and the land-army commander Tigranes were slain.
